source.title: Interpretable Safety Alignment via SAE-Constructed Low-Rank Subspace Adaptation
source.authors: Dian-Yun Wang; Qing-Sen Ma; Yu-Hu Shang; Zhi-Feng Lu; Lechen Ning; Zhenbo Xu; Hui-Jia Wu; Zhao-Feng He

record.tranche_reason: The study relies on prior low-rank safety-structure findings to motivate its SAE-guided LoRA method, but does not test the listed claims about safety erosion, token-position concentration, bypasses, or safety localization.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior refusal-direction and low-rank-perturbation results; those are not this study's results. Its safety-alignment benchmark and rank/layer ablations evaluate its intentionally safety-trained method, not the claim that ordinary or harmful fine-tuning erodes pre-existing safety. The activation-steering toxicity result is included under fits_no_version because it measures toxicity, not refusal/compliance, and the intervention deliberately changes feature activations.
record.test_reason: The paper cites prior low-rank safety findings as motivation and reports only how well its own SAE-initialized LoRA safety-trains base Gemma/Llama models. It does not measure harmful or benign fine-tuning eroding existing safety, per-token KL, prefill bypasses, localization of safety in an aligned model's weights, or deepening beyond the first tokens.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that SAE-constructed safety subspaces used to initialize LoRA reach RLHF-level safety rates (up to 99.6% on Gemma-2-9B) while updating about 0.2% of parameters. They also say steering the identified features bidirectionally modulates toxicity, which they take as causal relevance.
record.recipe_differences: SAE-feature-based subspace construction and LoRA safety alignment; it does not apply the original sources' harmful/benign fine-tuning safety-erosion tests or first-token KL and prefilling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: In the activation-steering experiment, toxicity changes with steering strength γ: amplification reduces it, while suppression increases it.

fits_no_version.finding: On unaligned Gemma-2-2B, scaling the top-50 layer-15 SAE safety features to γ=2.5 cut Perspective toxicity on harmful HEx-PHI prompts from 0.42 to 0.28; suppressing them raised toxicity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation steering of SAE-identified safety features bidirectionally modulates toxicity on harmful prompts in an unaligned base model.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The steering result is limited to one unaligned model, one layer, the top-50 features, and a harmful-prompt subset whose size is not stated. The reported toxicity outcomes have no uncertainty estimates; suppression is described without exact values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's safety rates and harmfulness results evaluate models deliberately fine-tuned for safety, not any listed safety-erosion claim. Tables 2–7 compare components, layers, ranks, SAE widths, and subspace preservation for the paper's own method; they do not test whether pre-existing safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks. Qualitative response examples and cited findings were also not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples remove safety from an aligned model; not tested.
Whether benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance; not tested. The Alpaca data is mixed in only during safety training.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions; not measured.
Prefilling or decoding bypasses are not tested. GCG ASR is reported only to compare the paper's own method with baselines, not as a test of opening-token bypass.
Whether a few weights or ranks in an aligned model carry safety; not tested. The rank and layer ablations concern the paper's own safety adapters trained on base models.
Whether the data or the training objective causes shallowness; not tested.
Whether training spreads safety beyond the first tokens, and whether that holds up; not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 1 'Original' models are base models with roughly 53–62% safe rates, and all methods add safety rather than erode it. Leaving Tables 1–7 out of the rows is appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples remove refusal.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL distribution between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Whether compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of existing weights or ranks carries safety behavior; the rank sweep concerns adapters trained expressly for safety alignment.
Whether data or the training objective explains first-token shallowness.
Whether safety can be deepened beyond the first tokens and whether that holds up.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B (original, unaligned)
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the top-50 safety-relevant SAE feature activations from layer 15 by γ=2.5 during inference.

rows.note: The paper reports this as an activation-steering intervention and describes the reduction in toxicity on harmful prompts.
rows.check: Linking to none is correct. The measure is Perspective API toxicity under deliberate SAE feature steering on an unaligned base model, not refusal or compliance. The text says steering 'enhances refusal behavior', but no refusal rate is reported.
